1:
That the reply came only after the whole speech is noticed on both sides. Gill has Job wait until Eliphaz had finished, without interrupting, though there was much in the speech that was provoking, and defends the right to answer as one every man has when his character is attacked. Henry draws the rule out of it, that anyone who would judge a discourse impartially must hear it out and take it entire. Gregory the Great makes the silence part of the trial rather than a courtesy. On his reading some men are wounded more by reproaches than by scourges, since the tortures of speech assail us worse than any pain and, while they stir us to vindicate ourselves, lay us low in impatience; so the friends' talk was added to the blows from above, sorer than the blows, to drive the holy man into wrath and defile his purity with pride of speech. His verdict is that the man gave thanks under the scourges and answered rightly when galled with words, though a few things in his words might seem to pass the limits of patience. He will weigh those only against the sentence of the Most High Judge, who set this servant above the adversary at the outset and afterwards rebuked the friends for not speaking the thing that was right as his servant had. Ellicott hears a man baulked of the sympathy he hoped for, from whom we must not expect the formal reply of a logical argument, since the friend has so misjudged the case as to be neither worthy of a direct answer nor able to take one in.

The request to have the grief weighed is read in several senses. Gill renders it weighed in weighing, as exactly as scales can do it, and lists what the thing weighed may cover: the affliction, the wrath behind it, the resentment those providences raised in Job's mind and broke out in hot expressions, the groans, or the impatience he stood charged with — and in every sense judicious men of moderate temper, weighing the trouble with the words, would make great allowance. Keil and Delitzsch put the two scales plainly, vexation in one and calamity in the other, and gloss the second noun from a root meaning to gape, so that it is properly a yawning gulf and then any dreadful disaster. Clarke turns the image into a demand for justice: let the sins be weighed against the sufferings if they can be proved, and if not, let the sufferings and the complaints be weighed together, when it will appear that bitter as the complaint was it was small beside the distress behind it. Wesley wants an equal judge who would understand the case and consider whether there was not cause for complaint. Henry has Job appeal past his friends to a third party with just weights, since he could not fully describe the calamity and they would not fully apprehend it.

The sand is a measure of two things at once. Clarke says so directly: the figure carries a number too great to count and a weight too great to estimate. Gill is particular about the physics: sand is heavy in itself, what lies on the shore is lighter for being dried by sun and wind, what is lifted straight out of the sea carries the added water, and the hyperbole asks us to imagine all the sand of all the seas outweighed by one man's affliction. On the words being swallowed up, Ellicott takes it that words are useless and powerless to express such a case, and Wesley that voice and spirit alike fail. Henry reads it as an apology offered in advance, that his friends must excuse both the brokenness and the bitterness of his speech and not expect the polish of an orator or the gravity of a morose philosopher.
4:
The arrows are taken as a figure with a medical body to it. Clarke reads them as poisoned shafts and describes the wound: a burning fever with parching thirst that dries the body's moisture, stops the salivary ducts, thickens and inflames the blood, and ends in a raging mania full of terrifying images from which only death relieves the patient. For the commonplace that Eastern writers make calamities God's arrows he quotes a saying he attributes to Aaly, the son-in-law of Mohammed: if heaven were a bow and earth its cord, calamities the arrows and mankind the mark, and God the unerring archer, where could the sons of Adam flee — the answer being, to the Lord. Gill distinguishes two senses and prefers the second. The outward strokes called God's arrows elsewhere had all fallen on this man — poverty, malignant ulcers, sheep destroyed by lightning — but what the verse means is rather the inward distress they raised, with a keen sense of the divine displeasure behind it. Wesley takes the poison for the distinguishing feature, arrows dipped in wrath as barbarous nations dipped theirs, so that they burn up the vital parts as well as pierce, and reads the terrors in array as an army invading on every side. His conclusion is that trouble of mind is the sorest trouble, and that here the sufferer was an eminent type of Christ, who complained most of the sufferings of his soul. Ellicott corrects the English, since the spirit imbibes the poison rather than the poison drinking up the spirit, and keeps the sense of hosts marshalling for battle.

The two animals are an argument, not an ornament. Gill has neither beast complain while pasture and provender last, so that a man who made no moan in such circumstances would be duller than the brutes; and he turns the comparison on the friends, who lived in tranquillity, as Aben Ezra observes, and did not roar. Clarke identifies the creature as the tame ass grown larger, stronger and swifter in the wild, and puts the argument as a question: do I complain without cause, when neither beast complains unless in want? Wesley reaches the same point from the friends' side, that men at ease have no occasion to complain, any more than this man had when he wanted nothing. Ellicott turns the figure forward into the next complaint, that a groan is evidence of a burden, so that the disdainful handling of it is itself insipid, and the proffered remedies are loathsome meat a soul refuses to touch.

The food completes the chain of comparisons. Gill instances the pulse that has no taste unless salted, and reads the verse either of the wormwood and water of gall the man was fed with or, as some apply it, of the friends' talk, unseasoned by the salt of prudence. Ellicott adds the alternative that the words rendered the white of an egg may mean the juice of purslain. Clarke prefers Mr. Good's rendering, which asks whether insipid food without salt, or the white of an egg, gives forth any pungency, and glosses it: a man with nothing provocative in his diet would be quiet, but this man's food is the very calamity most acute to his soul. Wesley puts the common-sense form of it, that men complain of merely unsavoury meat, and how much more of meat as bitter as this. On the refused dish Gill gives two senses, the food once too mean to touch and now gladly eaten — with a Jewish reading that what he would not have wiped his hands on now served as a tablecloth for his bread of sorrow — or, as he prefers, the friends' words, loathed like rotten provisions. Wesley's reading of the same verse is the plainest: the afflictions he once dreaded the thought of are now his daily bread.
8:
The request is for death, and the commentators differ on how to take that. Gill works through the senses of the verb, the petition going up to the ears of the Lord or the thing petitioned for coming back to the petitioner, and notes that death is elsewhere pictured as a person looking in at the windows. Ellicott sees a turn from men to God which is not quite faith, the hope being rather from God than in God, and generalises it: this is the language of all sufferers who assume that relief must come by a change of circumstances rather than in themselves. His quiet correction is that with God and in God there were many years of life and prosperity still in store, while the sufferer was calling death his expectation. Henry is the severest, holding that ungoverned passion grows more violent for being checked, as the sea rages most against a rock, so that a man reproved for courting death says it again with more vehemence — words recorded for our admonition and not our imitation. Yet Henry marks the limit he kept: desirous of death and angry at its delays, he never offered to take his own life, and the morals that recommend self-murder as a redress for insupportable grievances were neither known then nor to be entertained by anyone who regards the law of God and nature.

The verbs of the ninth verse are read closely. Gill insists the destruction asked for is of the body only, not of body and soul, which was a terror to this man, and not annihilation but the dissolving of the union between them; the word means to bruise and beat to pieces, so that the house of clay crumbles into its original dust, which is why Mr. Broughton renders it a bringing down to the dust. Clarke takes the loosing of the hand for an archer's gesture, the string drawn to the head and the hold then released so that the arrow may fly to its mark. Wesley's whole note is that the asking is to have days and calamities ended together.

The comfort expected from that stroke is where the chapter becomes hardest to construe. Gill allows two times for it, either before death, in the view of its nearness, so that a man might exult in his afflictions and sing on the brink of eternity, or after death. Henry reads it as the hope the righteous have in dying, which a man without a good conscience could not have spoken with such assurance, and draws from it the vanity of a life so uncertain that it often becomes its owner's heaviest burden. On the hardening, Henry will not follow him: we should soften ourselves under sorrow so as to take its good impressions, and daring the Almighty to spare nothing is great presumption, since we are not stronger than he. Clarke takes the same words as resolution rather than defiance, a man who knows his misery will shortly end enduring the present with determination, and not resisting a decree that must be just because its author is holy; and he reports three manuscripts of Kennicott's and De Rossi's reading this rather than yet, so that the clause runs, and this should be my comfort. Ellicott calls the sequence of thought obscure, singles out the phrase about hardening as the most doubtful in the verse since it occurs nowhere else in scripture, and lists the renderings offered: exulting in pain that spares not, burning in sorrow, or the received reading, which he prefers. On the last clause Ellicott glosses concealing as denying and finds the same confidence in the Psalmist; Wesley expands it into a profession of the true religion kept up without shame in the midst of heathens, so that being cut off would leave the man a gainer.
11:
The question about strength is aimed at something Eliphaz had promised. Gill takes it of the restoration of health that had been held out, and offers two other senses of the verb besides hoping, bearing a load to which his strength was unequal and simply continuing. Clarke makes the two halves of the verse a single argument: a man who cannot suppose his strength will return, and who would still have no prospect of a happy end if it did, has nothing left to bear his present ills with. Ellicott notes that the second clause is literally about prolonging life, though some take it as being patient, in the sense our word long-suffering carries. Keil and Delitzsch read the question as asking whether a wasted strength and a certain unhappy end do not make calm waiting as impossible as it is useless, and gloss the idiom of drawing out the soul as spreading the intensity of feeling out, which is forbearance. Wesley says the same of the strength and then answers the question about the end in the sufferer's own voice, that death is not terrible to him but comfortable, so why should he wish to prolong anything. Wesley also carries the observation that the man never offered to put an end to his own life, that no one with regard for the law of God and nature would entertain such a thought, and that however uneasy the soul's lodging in the body it must not break prison but wait for a fair discharge.

The stones and the brass draw out a classical parallel. Gill asks whether this strength is like the foundation and corner stones that carry a building, or like a pillar that will bear a prodigious weight, and answers that it is not. Clarke calls the figure proverbial in all countries and brings two witnesses for it. From Cicero he takes the saying that a man is not chiselled out of rock nor hewn out of oak but has a body and a soul, the one moved by the senses and the other by the mind. From Homer he takes the scene where Apollo urges the Trojans on by telling them that the enemy are not rock nor ribbed with steel, so that weapons will enter and strokes be felt, which Clarke gives in Pope's version and calls almost the same expressions as these. Wesley reduces it to the plain claim, that a man of flesh and blood like other men cannot endure such miseries longer.

The last question of the paragraph is the obscurest, and they answer it three ways. Gill reads it as a claim, since the word may mean defence: it is in the sufferer's power to defend himself against the calumnies cast on him, and though he has no strength to lift his burdens he has a good conscience and the force of argument on his side. Clarke reads it the opposite way, a confession that his help is all in himself and therefore perfect weakness, with friends gone, property gone and nothing stable left; but he is emphatic that the man neither said nor meant that reason had been driven from him, and that there is no mark in the chapter of a mind deranged. Ellicott will not choose. He offers two constructions, one making it a bare statement that there is no help in him and wisdom is driven quite away, the other making it causal, that because there is no help in him wisdom is therefore being driven far off — by the friends' reproaches and insinuations. Wesley takes the same indignant sense: a helpless outward condition is no proof of a lost understanding, and the man can still judge whether it is better for him to live or die, whether he is a hypocrite, and whether his comforters' words have any weight or their method any rightness in it.
14:
Pity is treated as a debt, not a kindness. Gill catalogues the afflictions that create the obligation — inward distress under a sense of God's displeasure, outward loss of health, goods and family, assault by Satan, persecution by men — and defines the pity owed as a sympathy of spirit shown in visiting, speaking comfortably and relieving need. Henry puts it as the least those at ease can do: take cognizance of a case, hear the complaints, mingle tears, and relieve what can be relieved, as becomes members of one body who do not know how soon the case may be their own. His second head is sharper: withholding compassion is irreligion, since the man who does it has forsaken the fear of the Almighty, and those who feel no pity for men under the rod plainly have no fear of it themselves. Wesley reads the opening word as melted or dissolved by affliction, and turns the clause back on the comforter as evidence that he is guilty of the very thing he had charged.

The second half of the verse is textually disputed, and the disagreement runs deep. Keil and Delitzsch render it as gentleness due to a man who is consumed, lest he forsake the fear of the Almighty, and report Ewald's supplying two lines as fallen out, which Hitzig called a pure swindle and they think unnecessary. Ellicott grants the difficulty of fixing the relation of dependent clauses in an archaic language, judges the English version wrong, and offers three constructions: even to one who forsakes the fear of the Almighty, or lest he should forsake it, or he may even forsake it. Clarke prefers the Latin, which makes the man who takes mercy from his friend the one who has cast off the fear of the Lord, and reports thirty-two of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts reading a different word in the first clause, so that shame falls on the man who despises his friend — which Clarke, following Mr. Good, thinks the comforter had deserved. He supports it with a classical tag about a sure friend being discerned in an unsure matter, which he says our own adage gives in full, and with a Latin satire, in Francis's version, against the man who tears an absent friend, will not defend him, courts cheap laughter, invents what he never saw, and cannot keep a secret.

The brook is the chapter's famous image, and each of them works it differently. Gill stresses that these were brethren by profession of the same religion among idolaters, which aggravates the treachery, and describes a channel fed not by a spring but by falls of water and melting snow, swelling for a season to look like a river. Clarke makes it the land torrent that appears suddenly after rains on the mountains and is as suddenly drunk up by thirsty sand, promising a permanent stream, watched with delight while people fill their tanks, and then failing before the tanks are full. Ellicott calls it one of the most celebrated similes in the book and vouches for it from his own travel, since the great river at Cordova, whose name means the mighty watercourse, was in August a third-rate stream in divided currents over a stony bed. Henry develops it in three stages: the show the brooks make when a land flood swells them, the expectation of thirsty travellers who have seen water there in winter, and the confusion of finding heaps of sand in the heat — his application being that everyone applauds the prosperous and fails them when they need help. Wesley closes with the counsel the image is meant to teach, that it is no new thing for brethren to deal deceitfully, and that we cannot expect too little from the creature or too much from the Creator.
16:
The frozen stage of the figure is read both physically and morally. Clarke keeps to the physics: water suddenly frozen, its foam turned to the likeness of snow or hoar-frost, then liquefied as soon as the heat comes and carried off so fast by evaporation above and absorption below that it simply disappears. Wesley adds the point of the season, that the channel is full when the traveller neither needs nor wants it, with the water of old snowfalls hidden under the ice, so that the verse is not about brooks fed by a constant spring but about those filled by accidental falls of water and snow. Gill allows the blackness two applications. It may describe the sufferer and his household, left in black and mournful circumstances and passed by, since the word is elsewhere rendered of those who mourn; or, as Gill prefers, it describes the friends themselves, foul water frozen over so that nothing can be seen through it, which answers to the blackness of their hearts under a fair outward appearance.

The vanishing is where the comparison bites. Gill reads the thaw as the hour of adversity: the sun of affliction looked on the sufferer and the friends melted away, or at least gave no comfort. Wesley marks the two words for the weather, the milder turn and then the hot season, when water is most refreshing and most needed. On the paths turned aside Gill has the melted water running off in small streams and windings until the very tracks of it are lost, which answers to a friendship of which no trace remains. Clarke notes that such channels sometimes desert their old beds altogether, as the Ganges frequently does, and that a stream divided into many smaller ones comes to nothing and is lost in the sand. Ellicott finds the clause ambiguous between the water and the travellers, since it may say that the paths of the streams are turned aside and come to nought, or that the caravans travelling by way of them turn aside into the waste and perish; the next verse inclines him to the second.

The caravans give the image its human weight. Gill identifies Tema as an Arabian city named from a son of Ishmael and the troops as trading companies, who in passing looked for supply at the places where they had seen great frozen waters in the winter. Clarke stages the arrival: men coming where torrents were known to descend from the mountains, confident of slaking their thirst and filling their water-skins, who find the water dissipated and are confounded because they had hoped. Ellicott supplies the geography from Fürst, Tema a tract in the north of the Arabian desert on the border of the Syrian one, where traffic ran by caravan from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean, and Sheba probably a district on the Arabian Gulf whose merchants traded with the distant cities of the East and also enriched themselves with their neighbours' plunder. Wesley explains why both names belong here, since each lay in the hot and dry part of Arabia where water was scarce and therefore precious, and why the travellers moved in companies rather than singly, for security against wild beasts and robbers. Keil and Delitzsch render the outcome in the two words the Hebrew gives it, that they were put to shame on account of their trust, and came so far only to be red with shame.
20:
The travellers' shame closes the simile. Gill has them ashamed not of the dry channel but of themselves, for raising expectations on so groundless a surmise. Ellicott refers the picture to Jeremiah's account of a famine, where men come to the pits and find no water. Wesley states the moral the figure was built for, that we prepare confusion for ourselves by our vain hopes, and that the reeds break under us because we lean on them.

The application to the friends turns on a disputed word. Gill reports the written text as the English has it, while the margin gives, ye are like it — that is, like the brook just described, as Jarchi takes it — and he commends Mr. Broughton for keeping both at once, that they had become like that, even nothing. Ellicott sets the same two readings side by side, either that they are become like that wady or that they are become nothing, and continues the second into the next clause, that they have seen an object of terror and are terrified. Keil and Delitzsch judge the received reading unsuitable and prefer the other, noting that the verb is not are but are become, and that the Targum renders it as having become as though they had never been. Clarke draws the parallel out: these men are to the sufferer exactly what the deceitful torrents were to the caravans, and what they see in him is a man swept from his eminence into want as a flood is carried off the mountains and lost in the desert. Both Clarke and Wesley read the fear in the verse as self-regarding, men starting back from the sight instead of drawing near to comfort, afraid either that the plagues might reach them through him or that he would prove a burden.

The four questions that follow are a defence, and the commentators take them as such. Gill reads them as asking whether he had ever invited them to come with presents in their hands, or to fetch him out of the hand of straitness. Clarke puts the same questions back to the friends — why stand aloof, when nothing was asked of your stores and no one was sent for to avenge the destruction of my property or recover my goods from my enemies. Ellicott hears the argument underneath them, that the sufferer had never laid himself under obligation nor asked help before, so that he cannot be convicted of having worn out their patience and brought this treatment on himself. Wesley supplies the two means that were never requested, deliverance by force of arms, as Abraham delivered Lot, and redemption by price or ransom, and adds what was wanted instead: comfortable words, when nothing else was expected. Henry makes the restraint a virtue and the neglect worse for it. The man had grounds enough to ask for a collection — losses that came by the hand of God and not by his own folly, a record of charity when he had the means, and friends with the ability to help — and he asked for none of it, because a good man in trouble is afraid of being troublesome. Nor did he ask them to raise the country, recover his cattle from the raiders, or make reprisals. Henry's conclusion is that not asking did not excuse them from offering, and that it aggravates their unkindness that what he did want was a good look and a good word, and he could not get either. His closing comparison is the chapter's best: from men, even when we expect little, we often have less, while from God, even when we expect much, we have more.
24:
The offer to be taught is read as evidence of temper rather than of doubt. Gill has the sufferer, his defence made and thought sufficient, nevertheless inviting instruction to show that he is not stubborn, and undertaking to acknowledge his mistakes if any are proved; and Gill turns it into a character of good men, who are not above instruction and will take knowledge from superiors, equals, and even inferiors — as here from friends who had used him hardly. The promise attached to the offer is silence: no interruption, no contradiction, but patient hearing and weighing of what is said. Clarke puts the same thing as a challenge to produce proper arguments, with a pledge to abandon any error he is convicted of, and Wesley reduces it to a demand for solid arguments and a promise to receive counsel gladly. Keil and Delitzsch render the second clause as a request to be made to understand where he has failed.

The praise of right words carries a sting, and the word itself is disputed. Gill expands the phrase into strong reasons and weighty arguments that bring their own evidence with them, and applies it above all to the words of God, which are not contrary to right reason though above it, and come with force when they come in the demonstration of the Spirit. Clarke agrees that a well-constructed argument founded on truth is irresistible, and then turns the second half on the comforters: their reasoning is defective because their premises are false, so that their conclusions prove nothing, and the clause means literally, what reproof is there in a reproof from you — since having proved no fault they have reproved no vice. Clarke also reports two manuscripts, with the Chaldee and some rabbins, reading how savoury or pleasant for how forcible, and judges both senses good but the common reading better. Keil and Delitzsch work the same crux harder, noting that the sweeter sense would suit this verse but not a later one, that Hupfeld compares a word for bitter and renders it however bitter, and that Hahn compares an Arabic verb for being sick to get the sense in what respect are right words bad — which they reject, since physical sickness and ethical badness are not nearly related ideas. Ellicott paraphrases the whole couplet into a preference for open rebuke over secret love, honest reproof being better than insinuations meant to pass for friendship. Wesley states it flatly: words of truth have a marvellous power, and there is no truth in these assertions nor weight in these arguments.

The complaint about reproving words is the chapter's sharpest piece of self-defence. Gill asks whether the whole device is to catch at a few expressions uttered in distress and make a man an offender for a word, and whether a charge of hypocrisy can be supported out of hasty speech without a single action from the man's life being produced against him. Clarke presses the same question and adds the circumstance, that a man complaining in the bitterness of his heart through despair of life is a strange subject for such advantage-taking, when no flaw can be found in his conduct. Ellicott turns it into an argument from the friends' own premises: they cannot mean to reprove mere words, which the sufferer admits his to be and which they themselves treat as nothing, since on that showing the words are hardly worth the trouble and might be left to answer themselves. Wesley allows what the others imply, that human infirmity and extreme misery deserve some allowance, and glosses the two terms of the verse, the desperate man as poor, miserable, hopeless and helpless, and words like wind as words that pass away and are forgotten.
27:
The charge of overwhelming the fatherless is applied to the speaker himself. Gill explains the figure: a man stripped of children, substance and health, helpless as an orphan and for a while given over into the hands of Satan, so that it was barbarous to press one already overwhelmed with sorrow. He then lists what may be made to fall upon the fatherless: their wrath, as the Targum takes it; a wall to crush him, per Aben Ezra; a lot, per Simeon bar Tzemach; or, as Gill prefers with Mr. Broughton, a net to entangle him in his talk. Clarke reads the halves as one accusation: men who see a friend as destitute as the most miserable orphan overwhelm him and lie in wait to catch him in his words. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both prefer a harder rendering, that they would cast lots over the fatherless and make merchandise of their friend, which Ellicott says better fits the language and keeps the parallelism. Wesley takes the loading as censures and calumnies, and adds the grievance behind it, that the sufferer had spoken his whole mind as to friends and they had used it to cast him down.

The appeal that follows is made in the language of courtesy. Gill renders the opening as a request that it may please them to look favourably on him and hear the case afresh, with no doubt of the acquittal. Clarke turns it into three imperatives, view me, consider my circumstances, compare my words, with the conclusion that they must then be convinced nothing but truth has been spoken. Keil and Delitzsch read the verb as observing scrutinizingly and the next particle as a negative asseveration, so that the sense is a refusal to deceive them to their face about the greatness of his suffering. Their rendering of the next summons is not retrace your steps but begin afresh, which they think suits both the clauses that follow it. Ellicott and Wesley agree on the substance, that the case is not to be treated as settled and the judgment given over again more righteously.

The last two verses are a demand for a rehearing. Gill offers a literal occasion for the word return, since the friends may have been rising from their seats to break off the conversation, and the request is that they sit down and resume the debate. Clarke makes it a reconsideration of the whole subject, with the clause about righteousness meaning that the argument itself is sufficient proof of innocence. Ellicott weighs whether the unrighteousness denied is in the case or in the tongue, prefers the latter on the strength of the next verse, and notes that the pronoun anticipates it. Wesley reads it the same way and puts the claim plainly, that the right will be found on the speaker's side in this matter between him and them. On the closing question Gill is careful, applying it to the particular words charged against him rather than to speech in general, since otherwise the tongue is a world of iniquity and the best of men offend in word. Wesley glosses the taste as the judgment, which tries words and actions as the palate tries meats. Clarke paraphrases it as a plea of honesty, that a conscience would have discerned a falsehood uttered in haste, and then speaks for himself: he has done what he could to keep the chapter's connection plain, without which much of it would be obscure, and he calls the whole an inimitable apology that might have ended the controversy had the friends not prejudged the cause. Ellicott ends on the same difficulty from the other side: the argument is hard to draw out in the logical form of Western thought, since the detail one must examine to explain it is what tempts a reader to take the speech piecemeal and lose the thread.
